extracted.intended_audience: educated British public, policymakers, and readers of political philosophy (late-18th-century audience)
extracted.subtask_description: A rhetorically argued political essay evaluating the French Revolution and the proper principles of government; it sets out standards by which governments, reforms, and revolutionary measures should be judged. The piece addresses moral, economic, institutional, and constitutional criteria for legitimate reform versus destructive revolution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protection of property and credit
rubrics_metrics.description: Government must safeguard property rights and public credit; confiscations and forced depreciated paper currency are 'so violent an outrage upon credit, property, and liberty' that they undermine the nation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Burke condemns wholesale confiscation of Church lands and compulsory paper currency as destructive to credit and property, describing compulsory paper circulation as an alliance of 'bankruptcy and tyranny.' Policies that confiscate or force depreciated paper as legal tender are flagged as both immoral and economically ruinous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect for existing institutions (avoid destroying institutions as a pretext)
rubrics_metrics.description: The service of the State must not be used as a pretext to destroy long-standing institutions (e.g., the Church); removing institutions for political ends is unjust and self-defeating.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Burke argues the Assembly refused a clergy offer because they desired to destroy the Church rather than make it serve the State; he treats the deliberate destruction of established institutions as a principal cause of national ruin.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prudence in disposing of large assets (avoid flooding markets)
rubrics_metrics.description: Large-scale, immediate sales of national property (e.g., Church lands) will depress values and harm the economy; sales should avoid sudden market saturation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay warns that bringing an 'unwieldy mass' of land to market at once would depress land values and divert circulating money from trade to land, thus defeating the expected profits and causing broader economic harm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid creation of a politically dependent landed interest
rubrics_metrics.description: Policies should not intentionally create a new landed interest beholden to the revolutionary regime, since such creation serves to bind supporters by interest rather than by principle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Burke notes that confiscation/sale schemes could create a new class of purchasers who hold estates on precarious political tenure, incentivized to extort and perpetuate the new regime for personal gain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preservation of judicial independence and legal continuity
rubrics_metrics.description: An independent judicature is an essential check; abolishing judicial bodies severs public justice from any check on central power and eliminates a refuge of ancient laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The abolition of the Parliaments is criticized as cutting off all appearance of connection between the crown and public justice. Burke emphasizes the risk that without these institutions people may lack a legal standard to appeal to and may be subject to arbitrary rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fairness in compensating holders of purchased offices or rights
rubrics_metrics.description: When offices or property rights (including those purchased) are altered or abolished, compensation must be just and not paid in worthless or sacrilegious currency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Burke criticizes compensating displaced magistrates or clergy in depreciated paper tied to confiscation funds, calling it degrading and effectively starvation for those owed justice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monetary stability and against compulsory depreciated tender
rubrics_metrics.description: A stable currency and voluntary transactions are essential; making revolutionary paper compulsory in payments is an intolerable violation that damages commerce and liberty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text condemns the compulsory acceptance of the new paper currency and links it directly to tyranny, bankruptcy, and the undermining of public confidence and economic life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Government judged by population and material prosperity
rubrics_metrics.description: The state of population growth and material wealth are reliable standards for assessing whether a government is overall harmful or beneficial to a country.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Burke asserts that flourishing population and accumulation of wealth (coin, public works, manufactures, arts) indicate that a government is not 'very mischievous' and that facts about population and wealth should temper denunciations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of mixed/tempered government over pure forms
rubrics_metrics.description: A mixed constitution—monarchy balanced by hereditary wealth/dignity and popular organs—is preferable to pure democracy or absolute monarchy; pure democracies risk party tyranny and oppression of minorities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Burke draws on classical authorities and practical judgment to argue that neither absolute monarchy nor absolute democracy is legitimate; a mixed system with checks is the desirable aim and what should have been preserved or reformed toward.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preference for reform over wholesale destruction
rubrics_metrics.description: If abuses can be corrected by reform, destroying the entire constitution is unjustified; reformation is to be preferred to pulling down 'the whole fabric at once.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Burke points to the original instructions to representatives calling for reform, not destruction, and warns that men have been 'led by degrees' into things they would not have permitted if they had foreseen the whole—so reformist motives should have been honored instead of revolutionary ruination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Against vilifying entire social orders (nobility/clergy) wholesale
rubrics_metrics.description: Broad denunciation of social orders (nobility, clergy) is both a libel and politically dangerous; critique should be specific and proportionate rather than erasing group identity and rights.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Burke defends many nobles and clergy as humane, hospitable, and public-spirited, and argues that painting them uniformly as villains justifies extreme retribution and social destruction that is unwarranted by fact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guarding minority rights against majority persecution
rubrics_metrics.description: A democracy can enable the majority to commit cruel oppressions upon a minority; constitutional design must guard against popular persecution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Burke warns that in democracies strong divisions lead the majority to exercise extreme oppression on minorities, producing sufferers in a more deplorable condition than under a single tyrant, because they are deserted by external consolation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure government's quality by cultural, infrastructural, and civic achievements
rubrics_metrics.description: The presence of arts, manufactures, roads, harbors, fortifications, learned men, and public charities are indicators that a government has fostered civilization and prosperity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Burke lists ports, canals, bridges, fortifications, manufactures, public foundations of charity, and learned professions as concrete evidence against claims that the old French government was utterly corrupt or incapable of reformation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rejecting ideological fanaticism and quackish parade
rubrics_metrics.description: Political actors who substitute theatrical fanaticism, show, and boastful rhetoric for sober policy (the 'quackish parade' of philosophical pretension) are to be distrusted and their measures suspect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Burke criticizes leaders intoxicated with their own wisdom who attempt to drown cries of indigence with tumult and rhetoric; he links such behavior to masking political failure and to moral and economic ruin.
